::: {.lead}
Today you work like in a lab: you summarize a long list in Excel, you ask
it new questions, and you test an AI summary of the numbers. Do each
experiment when your teacher shows it. After each step, write your result
in its box. At the end, copy your key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a computer with Excel (the desktop app, or Excel on the web
  at `office.com`) and an AI assistant that the university allows (for
  example Microsoft Copilot with your university account).
- **Time:** about 40 minutes for the three experiments.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. On the
  interactive lesson, every step has "Check your result". Look only after
  you try.

{{< start-files >}}

## Experiment 1 · A PivotTable

**Aim:** make a summary table of a long list in a few clicks. *(Lesson
notes 10.1 · about 10 minutes)*

1. Open `month-start.xlsx` (click **Enable Editing** if you see it). Click
   one cell of the list. Choose **Insert › PivotTable** and click **OK**.

   {{< record "Where is the PivotTable? What is on the right?" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Excel adds a **new sheet** with an empty PivotTable. The **PivotTable
   Fields** pane on the right lists the headings of the list: Week, Item,
   Type, Qty and Total (JD).
   :::

2. In the pane, drag **Type** to **Rows** and **Total (JD)** to **Values**.

   {{< record "Paper … ; Drinks … ; Bags … ; Grand Total …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Paper 206, Drinks 71, Bags 78; Grand Total 355 JD.** One row for each
   type, and the sum of its totals. Paper sold the most.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · New questions, same table

**Aim:** change the rows, the chart and the calculation, and keep the table
up to date. *(Lesson notes 10.2 · about 16 minutes)*

1. Drag **Type** out of Rows, and drag **Week** into Rows.

   {{< record "Weeks 1 to 4: … ; the best … ; the weakest …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **87, 63, 112 and 93 JD.** The **third** week was the best, and the
   **second** the weakest. The Grand Total stays 355 JD.
   :::

2. Click a cell of the PivotTable. Choose **PivotTable Analyze ›
   PivotChart**, then **Line**, and click OK.

   {{< record "Where does the line go down?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   From **week 1 to week 2** (87 → 63) and from **week 3 to week 4** (112 →
   93). A line chart shows a change over time.
   :::

3. Go to the sheet **March**. Change the total of the bag in week 3 from
   **48** to **58**. Look at week 3 in the PivotTable. Then choose
   **PivotTable Analyze › Refresh**.

   {{< record "Week 3 before Refresh … ; after Refresh …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **112** before Refresh, **122** after. A PivotTable does not change by
   itself: you refresh it after a change. Now change 58 back to **48** and
   refresh again.
   :::

4. Put **Type** in Rows again (instead of Week). Click **Sum of Total
   (JD)** in Values, choose **Value Field Settings**, then **Average**.

   {{< record "Average sale: Paper … ; Drinks … ; Bags …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Paper 20.6, Drinks 7.1, Bags 19.5 JD.** Paper has the biggest average
   sale. The same list answers a new question.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · An AI summary

**Aim:** let an AI tool describe the numbers, then check every number with
the PivotTable. *(Lesson notes 10.3 · about 14 minutes)*

1. Set the Values back to **Sum** (Value Field Settings › Sum). Select the
   PivotTable and copy it. In the AI assistant, type *Write three short
   sentences about these sales of March, each with a number:* and paste
   the table.

   {{< record "Numbers that are right … ; wrong or invented …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Check each number with the table: Paper **206**, Drinks **71**, Bags
   **78**, total **355** JD. If the AI writes a share, check it with a
   calculator (Paper: 206 ÷ 355 ≈ 58 %). Delete or correct every wrong or
   invented number. The table has no personal data, so you may paste it.
   :::

2. Open **Summary Check** on the interactive lesson. Mark each of the six
   sentences true or wrong.

   {{< record "The wrong sentences" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Wrong:** "Bags sold the most" (Paper did, 206 JD); "sales grew every
   week" (the second week fell); "the biggest sale was a bag for 48 JD"
   (the notebooks, 60 JD). The other three are true.
   :::

3. Write your own summary under the PivotTable or in Word: three true
   sentences, each with a number, and one sentence of AI-use statement.

   {{< record "My best sentence, and my AI-use statement" lines=3 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good summary: "March sales were 355 JD. Paper sold the most, 206 JD.
   The best week was the third, with 112 JD." A good statement: "I used
   Copilot for a first draft and checked every number with the
   PivotTable."
   :::
